title: Interviews and adverse inferences
subtitle: Sections 34 to 37 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994
objectives: Explain the s 34 inference from a failure to mention a fact later relied on at trial, including the effect of the suspect having had no legal advice at interview
State the s 35 inference that may arise from a defendant's refusal to give evidence at trial
Apply the s 36 and s 37 special-caution inferences to fact patterns involving an unexplained object, substance, mark, or presence at a scene

leadingAuthorities.role: Inference from a defendant's failure to give evidence at trial

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Adverse inferences sit exactly where criminal practice meets tactics: they change what a solicitor advises a client to do in the interview room, not just what happens afterwards in court.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You likely know each section's label already. This lesson is entirely about matching the right inference power to the right fact pattern under pressure — expect scenarios that mix up s 34, s 35, and s 36/37 deliberately.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Fix the four sections firmly before attempting the application material: s 34 is about silence on a fact later relied on, s 35 about not testifying, and s 36/37 about specific unexplained objects, marks, or presence. Confusing these four is the single most common error on this topic.

overview.hook: A suspect says nothing in interview, on their solicitor's advice, and months later stands trial and tells a detailed, apparently credible story for the first time. The jury is allowed to wonder: if that story were true, why keep it to yourself when it mattered most? That is what an adverse inference is — not proof of guilt, but permission for the fact-finder to hold a suspect's earlier silence against the account they later choose to give.

parts.heading: The s 34 inference: silence that comes back to bite
parts.voice: structural — sets out the core mechanism first
body: Section 34 CJPOA 1994 allows a court or jury to draw an adverse inference where a defendant, during police questioning or on being charged, failed to mention a fact that they later rely on in their defence at trial — provided that fact is one the defendant could reasonably have been expected to mention in the circumstances at the time.

The logic is not that silence itself is suspicious in the abstract. It is narrower and more specific: if a fact genuinely explains your conduct, and you had it available to you at interview, common sense suggests you would usually mention it then rather than saving it for trial — unless there is a good reason not to.

The inference only bites on facts the defendant later relies on. Staying silent about something never raised at trial at all triggers nothing under s 34 — the section is squarely about the gap between what was said (or not said) at interview and what is argued at trial.

components.definition: A conclusion the court or jury may draw against a defendant who failed to mention, when questioned or charged, a fact later relied on in their defence, where that fact was one they could reasonably have been expected to mention at the time.

interaction.prompt: A defendant said nothing at interview about a fact, and never mentions that fact at trial either. Can a s 34 inference be drawn?
options: No — s 34 only applies to facts the defendant later relies on at trial
Yes — any unexplained silence at interview can found a s 34 inference regardless of what happens at trial
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Without a fact later relied on at trial, there is nothing for s 34 to compare the earlier silence against.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what s 34 actually requires: a fact the defendant later relies on at trial. Silence about something never raised at trial at all does not trigger the section.

parts.heading: Legal advice to stay silent: why it usually blocks the inference
parts.voice: explanatory — resolves a genuine tension in the doctrine
body: A defendant is entitled to legal advice, and a solicitor is entitled to advise silence. So how does s 34 avoid punishing suspects simply for taking sound legal advice? The answer lies in the phrase 'could reasonably have been expected to mention' — the court considers all the circumstances, including whether the suspect had access to legal advice and what that advice was.

Where a suspect genuinely relied on, and acted on, proper legal advice to remain silent, courts are generally reluctant to draw an adverse inference, because it would then not be reasonable to have expected the suspect to have mentioned the fact at the time — reasonableness has to account for the advice actually given.

This is not an absolute bar, though. If the advice itself looks like a tactical device rather than a genuine attempt to protect the suspect — for example, where no coherent reason for the advice can be identified — a court can still draw an inference. The presence of legal advice shifts the analysis; it does not automatically switch the inference off.

components.label: What courts weigh when advice to stay silent is raised
points: Was the advice genuine legal advice, properly given, rather than a formality
Did the suspect genuinely rely on that advice, rather than having their own independent reason to stay silent
Was there an identifiable, legitimate reason for the advice on these facts
All the circumstances at the time — not simply the fact that a solicitor was present

interaction.prompt: A suspect stays silent throughout interview, genuinely and reasonably relying on their solicitor's advice that they were too unwell and confused to give a reliable account. At trial, the suspect relies on a fact never mentioned at interview. Is a s 34 inference likely?
options: Unlikely — genuine reliance on sound legal advice, for an identifiable legitimate reason, generally means it was not reasonable to expect the fact to be mentioned at the time
Certain — any silence at interview automatically triggers an inference regardless of advice
Unlikely, but only because the suspect was unwell, which is itself a separate defence
Certain — legal advice is irrelevant to the reasonableness question
interaction.explanation: Genuine, well-founded legal advice is exactly the circumstance s 34's reasonableness test is built to accommodate — the court asks whether it was reasonable to expect disclosure given everything that was actually going on, including sound advice not to speak.

parts.heading: Section 35: silence at trial itself
parts.voice: Socratic — separates this from s 34 by contrast
body: Section 34 is about silence at the police station. Section 35 is a different, later moment: a defendant's failure to give evidence at their own trial, or their refusal without good cause to answer a question once they have begun giving evidence.

Where the prosecution has established a case to answer, and the defendant, without good cause, does not testify, the court or jury may draw such inferences as appear proper from that failure. 'Without good cause' matters — a defendant who does not testify because of a recognised medical or mental condition affecting their ability to give evidence is treated differently from one who simply chooses to stay silent for no stated reason.

It's worth pausing on why this exists at all: a defendant is under no formal compulsion to testify, and the burden of proof never shifts to them. What s 35 changes is not the burden, but what a fact-finder is permitted to make of unexplained silence once the prosecution has already put forward a case that calls for an answer.

components.title: s 34 vs s 35: where the silence happens
components.description: A quick contrast to stop the two sections being conflated.

nodes.label: s 34 — silence at police interview about a fact later relied on at trial
s 35 — failure to give evidence, or answer a question, at trial itself

components.textAlternative: Section 34 concerns silence during police questioning about a fact later relied on at trial. Section 35 concerns a separate, later stage: the defendant's own failure to give evidence, or to answer a question, once the trial itself is under way.

interaction.prompt: A defendant, without any stated medical or psychological reason, declines to give evidence at trial after the prosecution has established a case to answer. Analyse whether a s 35 inference may be drawn.
factsToOrder: The prosecution has established a case to answer
The defendant does not give evidence
No medical or mental condition is stated as the reason
No good cause for the failure to testify is otherwise identified

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the court or jury may draw an adverse inference from the defendant's failure to give evidence.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 35, where the prosecution has established a case to answer and the defendant, without good cause, fails to give evidence, the court or jury may draw such inferences as appear proper from that failure.
modelAnswer.application: The prosecution has already established a case to answer, satisfying the threshold condition. The defendant has not testified, and no medical, mental, or other good cause has been identified for that failure.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, a s 35 inference is available to the court or jury, since the conditions for drawing one are met.

parts.heading: Sections 36 and 37: the special-caution inferences
parts.voice: case-narrative — anchors the rule in a concrete fact pattern
body: Sections 36 and 37 are narrower, more mechanical siblings of s 34, dealing with two specific situations. Section 36 applies where a police officer finds an object, substance, or mark on the suspect's person, clothing, footwear, or elsewhere, and reasonably believes it may be attributable to the suspect's participation in the offence. Section 37 applies where the suspect was found at or near the scene of the offence at or about the time it was committed.

In both cases, before an inference can be drawn, the officer must administer a 'special caution' — telling the suspect what the object, mark, or presence is, that the officer believes it may be attributable to their involvement, that the suspect is being asked to account for it, and that a failure or refusal to do so may harm their defence at trial. Without this special caution being properly given, no inference under s 36 or s 37 is available at all.

Picture a suspect stopped near a burgled property shortly after the alarm was raised, with fresh mud on their shoes matching the garden of the property. If, after a properly administered special caution, the suspect offers no explanation for either the mud or their presence nearby at that time, a court may draw an inference from that silence under s 36 (the mark) and s 37 (the presence) separately.

components.citation: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, s 36(1)
components.text: Where a person is arrested by a constable... and there is (i) on his person; or (ii) in or on his clothing or footwear; or (iii) otherwise in his possession; or (iv) in any place in which he is at the time of his arrest, any object, substance or mark... and the constable reasonably believes that the presence of the object, substance or mark may be attributable to the participation of the person arrested in the commission of an offence... and the constable informs the person arrested that he so believes, and requests him to account for the presence of the object, substance or mark... then... the court or jury... may draw such inferences from the failure or refusal as appear proper.
elements: Object, substance, or mark found on the person, clothing, or nearby
Constable reasonably believes it may relate to the offence
Special caution given, explaining the belief and inviting an account
Suspect fails or refuses to give an account

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is more clearly a s 37 (presence at a place), rather than a s 36 (object, substance, or mark), situation?
interaction.scenarioA: A suspect is found with paint transfer on their jacket matching a vandalised wall, and gives no explanation after a special caution.
interaction.scenarioB: A suspect is found standing directly outside a warehouse minutes after a break-in alarm sounds, and gives no explanation for being there after a special caution.
interaction.explanation: B concerns the suspect's presence at or near the scene at the relevant time, which is precisely what s 37 addresses. A concerns a physical mark connected to the offence, which falls under s 36 instead.

parts.heading: Matching the fact pattern to the right section
parts.voice: direct — trains the discrimination skill the exam actually tests
body: Most SQE1 errors on this topic come from applying the right idea to the wrong section, not from misunderstanding adverse inferences altogether. The discriminating question is always: at what stage, and about what, was the suspect silent?

If the silence is at the police station, about a fact later relied on at trial, think s 34. If the silence is the defendant simply not testifying at their own trial, think s 35. If the silence is a failure to explain a specific object, mark, or presence, after a special caution was properly given, think s 36 or s 37 — and note that s 36 and s 37 can apply together on the same facts if both an object/mark and a presence issue are in play.

One more distinction worth holding onto: s 34 requires no special caution — the ordinary caution given on arrest is enough, because s 34 turns on ordinary silence about a fact, not on a specific request to account for something concrete. Sections 36 and 37 are the ones that demand that extra, specific warning before they can operate at all.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume the ordinary caution given at arrest is sufficient to trigger a s 36 or s 37 inference, since it mentions that anything said may be used in evidence.
components.whyItsWrong: Sections 36 and 37 require a distinct special caution: identifying the specific object, mark, or presence, stating the officer's belief that it may be attributable to the suspect's involvement, and warning that a failure to explain it may harm the defence. The ordinary caution alone does not satisfy this and no s 36/37 inference is available without it.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that determines whether a s 36 inference is available here.
interaction.scenarioText: A suspect is arrested with what appears to be stolen jewellery in a bag. The officer says only the ordinary caution on arrest and does not explain the belief about the jewellery or invite an account. At the station, the suspect is asked no further questions about the bag.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That is the fatal gap. Without the special caution specifically identifying the item, the officer's belief, and inviting an account, s 36 simply does not engage, however suspicious the jewellery looks.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on what warning was actually given, not on how suspicious the jewellery looks. A s 36 inference depends on the special caution having been properly administered — the ordinary arrest caution is not enough.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following best describes the trigger for a s 34 adverse inference?
options: The defendant failed, when questioned or charged, to mention a fact later relied on in their defence at trial, which they could reasonably have been expected to mention
The defendant simply chose not to speak to the police at all, regardless of what happens at trial
The defendant refused to give a DNA sample
The defendant changed solicitors between interview and trial
testPool.explanation: Section 34 turns specifically on the gap between silence at interview and a fact later relied on at trial — not on silence in the abstract.

testPool.prompt: A suspect stays silent at interview after genuinely and reasonably relying on sound legal advice, given for an identifiable legitimate reason. Which statement best reflects the effect of that advice on a subsequent s 34 inference?
options: It is a highly relevant factor: reasonableness is assessed in light of the advice actually given, and genuine reliance on sound advice generally weighs against drawing an inference
It has no effect at all — legal advice is irrelevant to s 34
It automatically and absolutely prevents any inference from ever being drawn
It only matters if the solicitor personally attends the trial to confirm the advice
testPool.trapExplanation: Both extremes are wrong: advice is not irrelevant, but nor is its presence an absolute bar. Courts weigh whether the advice was genuine, properly given, and actually relied on when deciding whether it was reasonable to expect disclosure at the time.
testPool.explanation: Legal advice affects the reasonableness question directly, without functioning as a blanket exemption from s 34.

testPool.prompt: At trial, a defendant relies for the first time on an alibi never mentioned at interview, despite having had every opportunity to raise it and no legal advice against doing so. Which inference is potentially available?
options: A s 34 inference, since this is a fact later relied on at trial that was not mentioned when reasonably expected
A s 35 inference only, because the alibi was raised at trial
A s 36 inference, because an alibi is like an unexplained object
No inference of any kind, because alibi evidence is always excluded from adverse inference rules
testPool.explanation: This is squarely a s 34 scenario: a fact first raised at trial, not mentioned at interview when it reasonably could have been, with no advice-based explanation for the omission.

testPool.prompt: Under s 35, what is the trigger for a potential adverse inference?
options: The defendant's failure, without good cause, to give evidence at trial once the prosecution has established a case to answer
The defendant's failure to attend the police station voluntarily
The defendant's decision to plead not guilty
The defendant's failure to provide a written statement before trial
testPool.explanation: Section 35 is about the defendant's own silence at trial, once a case to answer has already been established — not about earlier stages of the process.

testPool.prompt: A defendant does not give evidence at trial because of a documented mental health condition that genuinely affects their ability to testify reliably. Is a s 35 inference straightforwardly available?
options: No — this is capable of amounting to good cause, which takes the failure outside the ordinary operation of s 35
Yes — s 35 applies regardless of any medical condition
Yes, but only if the defendant also declined to be interviewed by police
No — mental health conditions are always irrelevant to any adverse inference provision
testPool.explanation: A recognised condition affecting the ability to give reliable evidence is treated differently from an unexplained refusal to testify, because it can amount to good cause for the purposes of s 35.

testPool.prompt: A suspect is arrested with a screwdriver in their pocket near a break-in. An officer says only, 'you don't have to say anything, but anything you do say may be given in evidence,' and does not mention the screwdriver specifically. The suspect says nothing about it. Can a s 36 inference be drawn from this silence?
options: No — the ordinary caution given does not satisfy the special-caution requirement under s 36
Yes — any caution at all is sufficient to trigger s 36
Yes — the screwdriver being found near a break-in is inherently enough
No — s 36 never applies to tools or implements, only to marks on clothing
testPool.trapExplanation: Suspicious circumstances are not a substitute for procedure. Section 36 requires a special caution that specifically identifies the object, states the officer's belief, and invites an account — the general PACE caution given here does not do that, so no inference is available.
testPool.explanation: Without the object being specifically identified and an account specifically invited, s 36 simply does not engage, regardless of how incriminating the object looks.

testPool.prompt: What must a special caution under s 36 or s 37 specifically communicate to the suspect?
options: The object, mark, or presence in question, the officer's belief it may relate to the offence, a request for an account, and a warning that failure to give one may harm the defence at trial
Only the standard words used in the ordinary arrest caution
The maximum sentence for the offence under investigation
The identity of any co-accused already arrested
testPool.explanation: The special caution has specific, mandatory content going well beyond the ordinary caution — identifying the item or presence, the officer's belief, the request, and the consequence of silence.

testPool.prompt: A suspect is found hiding in bushes directly behind a shop shortly after its alarm sounds. After a properly administered special caution explaining the officer's belief and inviting an account, the suspect offers no explanation for being there. Which inference power is most directly engaged?
options: Section 37, since this concerns the suspect's presence at or near the scene at the relevant time
Section 34, since this happened at the point of arrest
Section 35, since it concerns testimony at trial
Section 36, since bushes count as an object
testPool.explanation: This is a presence-at-a-place scenario, which is precisely what s 37 addresses, distinct from s 36's focus on an object, substance, or mark.

testPool.prompt: Can s 36 and s 37 both apply on the same set of facts?
options: Yes — where both an unexplained object, substance or mark and an unexplained presence at the scene are involved, both sections can operate together
No — only one of s 36 or s 37 can ever apply to a single suspect
No — s 36 and s 37 are mutually exclusive alternatives chosen by the prosecution
Yes, but only if the suspect has no legal representation at all
testPool.explanation: Sections 36 and 37 address distinct features of a scenario (an object/mark, and presence at a place) and can both apply where both features are genuinely present on the facts.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following most accurately distinguishes s 34 from s 36 and s 37 in terms of the caution required?
options: Section 34 operates on the basis of the ordinary caution; s 36 and s 37 require a specific special caution before any inference is available
All three sections require exactly the same caution wording
Section 34 requires the special caution; s 36 and s 37 do not require any caution at all
None of the three sections require any caution to be given
testPool.trapExplanation: It is easy to assume the more procedurally demanding sections must be s 34, since it is the one most often discussed first. In fact it is the reverse: s 34 relies on the ordinary caution, while the narrower, more specific s 36/37 powers carry the extra special-caution requirement.
testPool.explanation: The special caution requirement is unique to s 36 and s 37 — s 34 does not need anything beyond the ordinary caution given on arrest.

testPool.prompt: A defendant mentions a fact at interview that they never rely on at trial. Separately, the same defendant does not give evidence at trial at all. Which inference provisions are potentially in play?
options: Section 35 only, since s 34 requires a fact later relied on at trial, which is absent here
Section 34 only
Both s 34 and s 35 equally
Neither section applies, since the defendant did mention something at interview
testPool.explanation: Section 34 has nothing to engage with here, since the fact was mentioned at interview and never relied on at trial. The failure to testify, however, squarely raises s 35.

testPool.prompt: Which of the following scenarios engages s 36 rather than s 37?
options: Blood staining is found on a suspect's sleeve, and after a proper special caution the suspect offers no account for it
The suspect is found standing at the entrance of a building shortly after an offence occurs there and gives no account for being there
The suspect fails to mention an alibi at interview that is later relied on at trial
The suspect declines to testify at trial without stating any reason
testPool.explanation: Blood staining is a mark on clothing — exactly the kind of object, substance, or mark that s 36 addresses, as distinct from presence at a place under s 37.

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly summarises the legal effect of an adverse inference under ss 34 to 37?
options: It permits the fact-finder to hold the silence against the defendant as part of the overall evidence, without shifting the burden of proof onto the defendant
It automatically results in a conviction unless the defendant can disprove the inference
It reverses the burden of proof, requiring the defendant to prove innocence
It has no practical effect on the outcome of a trial
testPool.explanation: An adverse inference is one piece of evidence the fact-finder may weigh — it does not convict on its own and does not shift the burden of proof, which remains on the prosecution throughout.

testPool.prompt: A suspect, properly special-cautioned about mud on their boots matching a burgled garden, gives a full and plausible explanation for the mud (recent gardening at home, supported by a receipt for compost bought that morning). Can a s 36 inference still be drawn on this point?
options: No — s 36 targets a failure or refusal to account; a genuine account has been given, so there is nothing for the section to bite on
Yes — any mud found near a crime scene automatically triggers the inference regardless of explanation
Yes, because the explanation must be verified by the court before it counts
No, because s 36 never applies to mud on footwear
testPool.explanation: Section 36 is triggered by a failure or refusal to account, not by the mere presence of a suspicious item. An account has been given here, so the section has nothing to operate on regarding this point.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is advising a client before interview. The client has a genuine, coherent account but the solicitor is confident it is true and simply prefers the client stays silent to see what evidence the police reveal first. The client stays silent on that advice, then gives the same account at trial for the first time. How is this advice likely to be treated for s 34 purposes?
options: It is less likely to protect against an inference, since the advice was tactical rather than grounded in a genuine reason connected to the client's ability to give a reliable account
It automatically protects the client in exactly the same way as advice given because the client was unwell or confused
It is irrelevant, since any legal advice at all blocks a s 34 inference
It guarantees an inference will be drawn, since tactical advice is always treated as bad faith
testPool.explanation: Courts distinguish advice genuinely connected to the suspect's situation from advice that is purely tactical, aimed at withholding a credible account to see the prosecution's hand first — the latter is less likely to prevent an inference being drawn.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring error is matching the wrong section to the fact pattern: silence at interview about a fact later used at trial is s 34, not testifying at trial is s 35, and an unexplained object/mark or presence — only after a proper special caution — is s 36 or s 37. Always ask: at what stage, and about what, was the suspect silent, and was the right caution actually given?
